questions.prompt: What actually happens inside a myofibril when a muscle cell contracts?
options: The actin and myosin filaments slide past each other, increasing their overlap
The actin and myosin filaments shrink and become physically shorter
The mitochondria shrink to make room for the cell to compress
The nucleus divides to create more space inside the cell
questions.explanation: Contraction is the sliding-filament mechanism: myosin heads grab actin and pull it inward, so the filaments slide over each other and overlap more, shortening the whole unit — without either filament changing length.
questions.misconception: It's easy to picture contraction like squeezing a sponge, where the material itself shrinks. But the filaments are rigid structures; it's their position relative to each other that changes, not their size.

questions.prompt: Why do muscle cells contain an unusually large number of mitochondria?
options: Contraction requires a constant, large supply of ATP for energy
Mitochondria store the calcium needed to trigger contraction
Mitochondria physically pull the actin and myosin filaments together
More mitochondria make the cell membrane stronger
questions.explanation: Sliding filaments and pumping calcium back out after each contraction both cost ATP. Muscle cells burn energy constantly, so they're packed with mitochondria to keep the ATP supply flowing.
questions.misconception: Students sometimes assume mitochondria play a direct mechanical role in contraction (like being part of the filament machinery), but their job is purely to supply energy — calcium storage is the sarcoplasmic reticulum's job, and the pulling is done by myosin.

questions.prompt: What role does the sarcoplasmic reticulum play in contraction?
options: It stores calcium and releases it to trigger the filaments to grip and pull
It generates the ATP that powers the contraction
It carries the electrical nerve signal into the cell
It is the outer membrane that separates the cell from its surroundings
questions.explanation: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is an internal calcium reservoir. When the signal to contract arrives, it releases a burst of calcium that exposes the binding sites on actin, letting myosin latch on and pull.
questions.misconception: It's often confused with the sarcolemma because the names sound alike — but the sarcolemma is the outer cell membrane that receives the nerve signal, while the sarcoplasmic reticulum is an internal structure that responds to that signal by releasing calcium.

questions.prompt: Why is it unusual, compared to most cells in the body, for a skeletal muscle cell to have many nuclei?
options: It's an adaptation to run a very large, long cell that needs to make lots of protein everywhere along its length
It's a sign the cell is diseased or dividing uncontrollably
Each nucleus controls a different, unrelated skeletal muscle cell
It only happens in cardiac muscle cells, never in skeletal muscle
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle cells can be very long (sometimes running the length of a whole muscle), and one nucleus can't efficiently manage protein production over that entire distance. Having many nuclei spread throughout the cell lets it support its own size.
questions.misconception: Multiple nuclei can look alarming, like a sign of abnormal cell division (as it would be in most other cell types), but in skeletal muscle it's a normal, healthy adaptation to the cell's unusual length and workload — and it's specifically a feature of skeletal muscle, not all muscle types.
